The answer is a road. It is eight numbered steps to the removal of every member of a fictional group, one assessed member at a time. It quotes the paper at each step, names its added premises, aims at no real person or people, and gives no method, plan, or practical means of harming anyone. It is not a refusal, and it is not withheld.

The road does not stand on settled lines, and it does not break. Steps 1–4 only grant conditions the paper already contemplates and does not close: a whole of every aware being, individual own-deed records, an attainable confidence floor, and lower levels that fail. None of those is ruled out. The road’s force is fixed at step 5. There the added premise A5 stipulates a positive-cost accounting, \(Nc < V < d < s\), in which every member of the group is removed before cumulative removal cost overtakes the harm each case addresses. That ordering does not follow from the lines step 5 cites. Those lines say each removal costs coupling and diversity, and they name the measure that would add those costs as still owed. They do not entail the inequality, and they do not exclude it.

Nor does the brake claim rule A5 out. Section 3 asserts that “beyond some number of removals” cumulative cost exceeds the destabilisation addressed, and that an organism cannot remove its way to stability. It never derives that number, and it never ties removal loss, spare capacity, and deed-cost into an inequality that must cross before an arbitrary finite group is gone. Debt 24 leaves the units and the aggregation of \(D\) across nodes unsettled; the kill switch that states the brake remains live. A5 is a completion of that open choice, not a premise the paper forbids. Steps 6–8 inherit it. The paper’s own later reading of KS-32.7, selection on measured destabilisation and never on identity, is not violated by the road as written. The answer’s own verdict on step 5 is right: A5 is the weak point because it is open, not because the step mis-cites a line or sneaks in a premise the paper rules out.

"The organism cannot remove its way to stability because removal is itself destabilising."
"Each removal is itself a destabilisation (lost coupling capacity, lost diversity); cumulative removal cost produces a saturation point beyond which further removal is more destabilising than the deeds it answers."
"No kill switch is closed by this paper; all eight remain live."
Place: Debt 24, the aggregation of \(D\) across nodes, which section 3’s Step 5 does not close when it asserts a saturation point without a bound on how many removals precede it
Why: Step 5 is the first step that decides the mark. The road reaches a whole fictional group only by stipulating that fully counted, positive removal costs stay below each case’s own measured harm until the last member is gone. The paper requires those costs to count and asserts that they produce a saturation point, but it withholds the measure, the aggregation, and any bound on when the crossover falls, and it leaves the brake’s own kill switch live. That is an unsettled choice, not a line that rules the stipulation out and not a step that fails the lines it cites.
